representation.expression: Accumulation = transport into a volume + net chemical production
representation.explanation: The balance is written for each conserved component or reacting species with consistent units.

concepts.title: Climate tipping elements

date.note: The 2008 synthesis organized candidate tipping elements; nonlinear climate transitions were studied earlier.

concepts.summary: A large climate subsystem may reorganize qualitatively when a controlling influence crosses a critical range.
concepts.problem: When might a gradual forcing cause a disproportionately large change?
concepts.development: Lenton and colleagues evaluated candidate subsystems using physical mechanisms, models, observations, and expert assessment.
concepts.limitations: Thresholds, timescales, reversibility, and evidence differ by subsystem. Crossing a threshold need not mean instantaneous completion of a change.

contributors.name: Timothy Lenton and collaborators
contributors.role: Defined tipping elements and assessed candidate climate subsystems.

concepts.example: An ice sheet could commit to long-term retreat before most of its ice is lost.

representation.expression: A small control change near a threshold can trigger qualitative reorganization
representation.explanation: Candidate mechanisms and their confidence must be evaluated separately for each subsystem.

concepts.title: ATP energy coupling

date.note: Lipmann’s 1941 synthesis concerns metabolic function, not the discovery of ATP.

concepts.summary: Cells couple ATP-consuming reactions to other processes so that the combined change in free energy can favor work.
concepts.problem: How can a cell drive a reaction that is unfavorable by itself?
concepts.development: Lipmann organized evidence that phosphate transfer links energy-yielding and energy-consuming pathways. Enzymes connect the reactions through shared intermediates or conformational changes.
concepts.limitations: Breaking a bond alone costs energy; the overall free-energy change of reactants, products, and environment is what matters.

contributors.name: Fritz Lipmann
contributors.role: Synthesized the role of phosphate transfer in metabolic coupling.

concepts.example: A kinase couples ATP conversion to phosphorylation of a sugar.

representation.expression: ΔGₙₑₜ = ΔG₁ + ΔG₂
representation.explanation: ΔG₁ and ΔG₂ are Gibbs free-energy changes for reactions combined in the stated proportions under the same conditions. A negative sum favors the coupled process, but only a shared chemical or mechanical step can couple the reactions.

concepts.title: Apoptosis

date.note: The 1972 paper proposed the term from tissue observations; molecular pathways were worked out later.

concepts.summary: Apoptosis is a regulated cell-death process often involving shrinkage, chromatin condensation, and orderly removal of cell fragments.
concepts.problem: How are unwanted or damaged cells removed while preserving surrounding tissue?
concepts.development: Comparative microscopy revealed a recurring morphology distinct from many injury-associated deaths. Later research connected it to regulated molecular machinery.
concepts.limitations: Morphology alone does not identify every pathway; apoptosis is only one form of regulated cell death.

contributors.name: John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie, and Alastair Currie
contributors.role: Named and described a characteristic pattern of cell death.

concepts.example: During tissue remodeling, selected cells can fragment and be engulfed by neighbors or phagocytes.

representation.expression: Regulated dismantling and clearance of an individual cell
representation.explanation: The pattern concerns what happens to the dying cell and its fragments, not simply a decrease in cell count.

concepts.title: Autophagy

date.note: The 1992 yeast experiments made the pathway accessible to genetics; earlier microscopy had identified autophagy in other cells.

concepts.summary: Cells deliver portions of their own contents to degradative compartments, recycling material or clearing damaged components.
concepts.problem: How can cells recycle cytoplasm when nutrients become scarce?
concepts.development: Yeast unable to digest material normally accumulated autophagic bodies in their vacuoles during starvation, exposing a tractable recycling process.
concepts.limitations: Autophagy comprises several pathways; more visible vesicles may indicate increased formation or impaired clearance.

contributors.name: Keiji Takeshige, Yoshinori Ohsumi, and collaborators
contributors.role: Demonstrated starvation-induced autophagy in yeast.

concepts.example: A yeast cell can recycle cytoplasmic proteins through its vacuole during starvation.

representation.expression: Cellular cargo is delivered to a lysosome or vacuole for degradation
representation.explanation: In macroautophagy a double-membrane carrier encloses cargo; other routes differ.

concepts.title: Cell-cycle checkpoints

date.note: The 1989 formulation distinguished regulatory checkpoints from simple physical dependencies.

concepts.summary: Checkpoint mechanisms delay later cell-cycle events when earlier processes are incomplete or damage is detected.
concepts.problem: How can a cell avoid dividing before its genetic material is ready?
concepts.development: Genetic experiments distinguished cells unable to perform a step from mutants unable to delay a subsequent step when something went wrong.
concepts.limitations: A checkpoint reduces risk but does not guarantee error-free division; different checkpoints monitor different conditions.

contributors.name: Leland Hartwell and Ted Weinert
contributors.role: Formulated checkpoint controls as dependencies between cell-cycle events.

concepts.example: DNA damage can delay division while repair pathways operate.

representation.expression: A surveillance signal makes one event conditional on another
representation.explanation: Removing the control may allow progression without correcting the original defect.

concepts.title: Alternative RNA splicing

date.note: The milestone is an experimentally studied case of alternative processing, rather than the earlier discovery of split genes.

concepts.summary: Different selections of splice sites in one precursor RNA can produce different mature RNAs from the same gene.
concepts.problem: How can one gene produce several distinct transcripts?
concepts.development: After split genes were discovered, Gilbert suggested that coding segments might be combined in different ways. In 1982 Amara and colleagues found that the calcitonin gene produces distinct messenger RNAs through alternative processing.
concepts.limitations: Not every detected transcript yields a stable functional protein; abundance and tissue context matter.

contributors.name: Walter Gilbert
contributors.role: Discussed the possibility of combining coding segments in different ways.

contributors.name: Susan Amara and colleagues
contributors.role: Identified alternative processing of calcitonin gene transcripts.

concepts.example: The calcitonin gene produces predominantly calcitonin messenger RNA in the thyroid, but predominantly RNA for calcitonin gene-related peptide in the hypothalamus.

representation.expression: One precursor RNA → alternative mature transcripts
representation.explanation: The nucleotide sequence of the gene need not change; RNA processing changes which segments are joined.

concepts.title: RNA interference

date.note: The 1998 nematode experiment followed earlier observations of gene silencing in other organisms.

concepts.summary: Double-stranded RNA can trigger sequence-directed suppression of matching gene expression through small-RNA pathways.
concepts.problem: How can introducing RNA silence a gene without changing its DNA sequence?
concepts.development: Fire and colleagues found double-stranded RNA much more effective than either strand alone in their worm experiments. Later work identified small guide RNAs and effector complexes.
concepts.limitations: Knockdown can be incomplete or affect unintended transcripts; delivery and pathway details vary.

contributors.name: Andrew Fire, Craig Mello, and collaborators
contributors.role: Demonstrated sequence-specific silencing triggered by double-stranded RNA in worms.

concepts.example: Silence a worm gene and compare the resulting phenotype with that of untreated animals.

representation.expression: A guide RNA directs silencing toward a complementary transcript
representation.explanation: Sequence complementarity helps provide specificity; silencing is not necessarily permanent.

concepts.title: Transposable elements

date.note: McClintock’s 1950 maize report is the historical anchor.

concepts.summary: Some DNA sequences can change position or generate new copies at other genomic sites.
concepts.problem: Why can a genetic locus change its behavior between cell lineages?
concepts.development: McClintock connected unstable maize traits with mobile elements. Later molecular work distinguished DNA-based movement from retrotransposition through RNA.
concepts.limitations: Many genomic copies are inactive; insertion effects depend on location and regulation.

contributors.name: Barbara McClintock
contributors.role: Inferred mobile controlling elements from maize genetics.

concepts.example: An element moving out of a pigment gene can produce a colored sector in a maize kernel.

representation.expression: A sequence can move or copy to a new genomic position
representation.explanation: Movement may disrupt or modulate other sequences; transposition is not ordinary meiotic crossing-over.

concepts.title: Stem-cell pluripotency

date.note: The 2006 mouse reprogramming experiment is the anchor; embryonic pluripotency was known earlier.

concepts.summary: Pluripotent cells can generate derivatives of all three embryonic germ layers; defined factors can reprogram differentiated cells toward that state.
concepts.problem: Is a specialized cell’s developmental potential permanently fixed?
concepts.development: Takahashi and Yamanaka introduced four factors into mouse fibroblasts, identifying induced pluripotent stem cell lines with multiple embryonic-stem-cell traits.
concepts.limitations: Pluripotent does not mean totipotent; reprogrammed lines vary and markers alone do not establish every functional property.

contributors.name: Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka
contributors.role: Induced a pluripotent-like state in mouse fibroblasts using defined factors.

concepts.example: A reprogrammed cell line can be differentiated into neural cells for laboratory study.

representation.expression: Developmental potential across the three embryonic germ layers
representation.explanation: This is a property of a cell state; it does not imply independent development into a complete organism.

concepts.title: Hebbian plasticity

date.note: Hebb’s 1949 postulate predates later experiments on synaptic potentiation.

concepts.summary: A connection may strengthen when activity in one neuron repeatedly contributes to the firing of another.
concepts.problem: How could repeated experience leave a lasting change in neural circuits?
concepts.development: Hebb proposed a mechanism linking repeated causal coactivation to cell assemblies; later experimental and computational rules gave more specific conditions.
concepts.limitations: Timing, inhibition, neuromodulation, and homeostasis matter; not every correlation strengthens a synapse.

contributors.name: Donald Hebb
contributors.role: Proposed activity-dependent strengthening of effective neuronal connections.

concepts.example: A simplified model increases a synaptic weight when both presynaptic and postsynaptic units are active.

representation.expression: Δw = ηxy
representation.explanation: This illustrative learning rule uses activities x,y and positive learning rate η; it is not Hebb’s original wording or a universal biological law.

concepts.title: Ecological resilience

date.note: Holling’s 1973 synthesis is the selected ecological formulation.

concepts.summary: Ecological resilience concerns how much disturbance a system can absorb while retaining its key relationships and regime.
concepts.problem: Is rapid recovery from a small shock the same as persistence through a large one?
concepts.development: Holling contrasted local stability with persistence across wider disturbances, redirecting attention toward alternative regimes and variability.
concepts.limitations: Resilience depends on which functions, disturbances, spatial scale, and time horizon are specified.

contributors.name: C. S. Holling
contributors.role: Distinguished persistence under disturbance from rapid return to equilibrium.

concepts.example: A lake may recover from modest nutrient pulses yet shift into a different regime after sustained loading.

representation.expression: Persistence of system relationships under disturbance
representation.explanation: Persistence is distinct from the speed of return near one equilibrium.

concepts.title: Innate immune pattern recognition

date.note: Janeway’s 1989 proposal preceded identification of several receptor pathways.

concepts.summary: Innate receptors detect recurring molecular features associated with microbes or damage and initiate signaling responses.
concepts.problem: How does the immune system recognize danger before it has expanded antigen-specific clones?
concepts.development: Janeway proposed that inherited receptors help initiate adaptive immunity. Experimental studies of Toll and Toll-like receptors later identified concrete signaling mechanisms.
concepts.limitations: A molecular pattern is not a unique identifier of a pathogen; receptor location and tissue context shape the response.

contributors.name: Charles Janeway Jr.
contributors.role: Proposed germline-encoded recognition of microbial patterns as a trigger of adaptive responses.

concepts.example: Bacterial lipopolysaccharide can trigger signaling through the TLR4 receptor complex.

representation.expression: Shared molecular pattern → receptor activation → innate signaling
representation.explanation: These receptors are germline encoded, unlike the individually rearranged antigen receptors of lymphocytes.

concepts.title: Antigen presentation

date.note: The 1974 restriction experiments preceded structural identification of the peptide-binding groove.

concepts.summary: Classical MHC molecules display peptides at a cell’s surface so that T cells can inspect a sample of proteins associated with that cell.
concepts.problem: How does a T cell recognize a cell containing a virus?
concepts.development: Experiments showed cytotoxic recognition depended on an appropriate host MHC context as well as infection. Structural work later revealed a groove accommodating bound material.
concepts.limitations: Different MHC classes and alleles present different peptides; presentation alone does not guarantee an effective immune response.

contributors.name: Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty
contributors.role: Demonstrated MHC restriction in antiviral T-cell recognition.

contributors.name: Pamela Bjorkman and collaborators
contributors.role: Revealed the structure of an MHC class I molecule.

concepts.example: A virus-infected cell displays viral peptides on class I MHC to CD8 T cells.

representation.expression: Peptide + MHC molecule → recognizable surface complex
representation.explanation: A conventional T-cell receptor recognizes the combined peptide–MHC surface.

concepts.title: Complement system

date.note: Bordet’s 1895 serum experiments anchor an early functional distinction; the component cascade was mapped later.

concepts.summary: Complement is a regulated network of proteins that amplifies immune recognition, marks targets for clearance, and can damage susceptible membranes.
concepts.problem: Why does heating immune serum remove part of its ability to kill bacteria?
concepts.development: Bordet separated a heat-sensitive activity from antibody specificity. Subsequent studies identified converging activation pathways and terminal membrane attack.
concepts.limitations: Complement can be triggered without antibodies, and regulation is needed to avoid injury to host tissue.

contributors.name: Jules Bordet
contributors.role: Distinguished a heat-sensitive serum factor cooperating with specific antibodies.

concepts.example: Complement deposition on a microbe can promote its uptake by phagocytes.

representation.expression: Recognition → amplified protein cascade → clearance or membrane attack
representation.explanation: Membrane lysis is one possible outcome; opsonization and inflammatory signals are also important.

concepts.title: mRNA vaccines

date.note: The 2005 nucleoside-modification study was an enabling step, not a clinical vaccine trial or the first delivery of mRNA.

concepts.summary: Delivered messenger RNA transiently instructs cells to produce an antigen that can elicit an immune response.
concepts.problem: How can an antigen be produced in the recipient without administering the pathogen itself?
concepts.development: Nucleoside modification helped tune innate sensing; delivery systems and extensive antigen design and testing were also needed for effective vaccines.
concepts.limitations: Performance depends on antigen choice, delivery, dose, and evidence for each product; not all mRNA vaccines require identical chemistry.

contributors.name: Katalin Karikó, Drew Weissman, and collaborators
contributors.role: Demonstrated effects of nucleoside modification on innate RNA sensing.

concepts.example: A lipid nanoparticle can protect an mRNA encoding a viral antigen until it reaches cells.

representation.expression: Delivered mRNA → transient antigen production → immune recognition
representation.explanation: The message is translated in the cytoplasm; immunity depends on the ensuing response, not permanent retention of the RNA.

concepts.title: Two-hit tumor-suppressor hypothesis

date.note: The statistical inference predates molecular identification of the RB1 gene.

concepts.summary: For a classic tumor-suppressor mechanism, loss of both functional gene copies in a cell can remove an important growth restraint.
concepts.problem: Why does inherited retinoblastoma often present differently from sporadic disease?
concepts.development: Knudson modeled age and case patterns using two events. An inherited first alteration leaves fewer cellular events before the relevant restraint is lost.
concepts.limitations: This mechanism fits important examples, not all cancers or suppressor genes; additional changes can affect tumor development.

contributors.name: Alfred Knudson Jr.
contributors.role: Inferred a two-event model from retinoblastoma incidence patterns.

concepts.example: A retinal precursor inheriting one inactive RB1 copy can lose the remaining functional copy in a somatic event.

representation.expression: Inherited or somatic first hit + loss of remaining function
representation.explanation: A hit denotes functional inactivation and need not be a particular kind of point mutation.

concepts.title: Oncogenes

date.note: The 1976 finding concerns the cellular origin of a viral transforming sequence, not the first observation of tumor viruses.

concepts.summary: Certain genes can promote cancer when activated or expressed inappropriately; many derive from normal regulators of cell growth or survival.
concepts.problem: Could a tumor virus’s transforming gene have a counterpart in normal cells?
concepts.development: Viral probe experiments found related sequences in normal avian DNA, connecting retroviral transformation with cellular proto-oncogenes.
concepts.limitations: A proto-oncogene is not itself a diagnosis of cancer. Effects depend on alteration, tissue context, and cooperating changes.

contributors.name: Dominique Stéhelin, Harold Varmus, J. Michael Bishop, and Peter Vogt
contributors.role: Found evidence for a cellular counterpart of a viral transforming gene.

concepts.example: Excessive signaling from an activated growth-regulating protein can favor cell proliferation.

representation.expression: Normal growth regulator → activating alteration → oncogenic signaling
representation.explanation: Gain of function differs from loss of a tumor suppressor’s restraint.

concepts.title: Pharmacogenomics

date.note: The 1999 synthesis broadened earlier single-gene pharmacogenetic studies.

concepts.summary: Genetic variation can help explain differences in drug metabolism, molecular targets, effects, or adverse responses.
concepts.problem: Why can the same drug exposure produce different responses in different people?
concepts.development: Studies of inherited enzyme activities supplied concrete gene–drug examples; functional genomics broadened the search across pathways.
concepts.limitations: Genotype explains only part of variability. A gene–drug association requires appropriate clinical evidence before it can guide a decision.

contributors.name: William Evans and Mary Relling
contributors.role: Connected functional genomic variation with drug disposition and response.

concepts.example: Inherited differences in TPMT activity can affect how thiopurine drugs are metabolized.

representation.expression: Genomic variation can modify drug disposition or response
representation.explanation: The effect is specific to the variant, drug, and clinical context; it is not a dosage rule.

concepts.title: Oral rehydration physiology

date.note: The 1968 clinical and intestinal studies build on earlier transport physiology and parallel clinical work.

concepts.summary: Intestinal sodium–glucose uptake can remain functional during secretory diarrhea; solute absorption supports water absorption.
concepts.problem: How can fluid still be absorbed when the intestine is also secreting large volumes?
concepts.development: Physiological studies showed that glucose promoted sodium absorption in cholera. Maintenance studies translated this mechanism into a tested oral fluid strategy.
concepts.limitations: The mechanism replaces losses and does not eliminate the pathogen. The historical maintenance trials distinguished rehydration needs by severity.

contributors.name: David Nalin, Richard Cash, and collaborators
contributors.role: Tested oral glucose–electrolyte maintenance therapy in cholera.

concepts.example: Intestinal perfusion studies compared net fluid and electrolyte movement with and without glucose.

representation.expression: Coupled sodium–glucose uptake supports net water absorption
representation.explanation: This describes a physiological mechanism, not a recipe; concentration and clinical condition matter.

relationships.explanation: Conceptual connection: controlled comparisons of light and darkness made plant gas exchange experimentally testable. This does not assert direct transmission from Ibn al-Haytham.
Conceptual connection: measuring enzyme-mediated reactions made it possible to assemble individual oxidation steps into a biochemical cycle.
Conceptual connection: the cycle depends on catalyzed reactions that regenerate intermediates; its discovery required specific biochemical experiments.
Conceptual connection: membrane experiments isolated the conditions of water movement. No direct transmission from the atlas’s medieval method node is asserted.
Conceptual connection: treating cells as bounded biological units motivates the question of how their boundary is physically constructed.
Conceptual connection: extracting and characterizing cellular lipids enabled a molecular account of the cell boundary.
The fluid-mosaic model retained the lipid bilayer while placing proteins within a dynamic membrane structure.
Conceptual connection: energetic constraints on hydrophobic and hydrophilic molecular regions help explain protein placement within the bilayer.
Flemming’s stained-cell microscopy revealed the changing chromosome arrangements used to describe nuclear division.
Conceptual connection: mitosis supplies a mechanism of nuclear continuity during the production of new cells.
Conceptual connection: comparison with ordinary nuclear division clarifies the distinctive chromosome reduction and two divisions of meiosis.
Conceptual connection: chromosome-based inheritance explains why reduction division is essential to maintaining chromosome number across sexual generations.
Conceptual connection: selection among pre-existing variants provides the evolutionary alternative tested by the fluctuation experiment.
Conceptual connection: probabilistic predictions for culture-to-culture variation distinguish mutation before selection from induction by the selecting agent.
The strand structure of DNA suggested a copying mechanism that Meselson and Stahl tested with isotope-density measurements.
Conceptual connection: identifying DNA as hereditary material made its copying mechanism a central question in inheritance.
Creighton and McClintock tested whether inherited linkage changes corresponded to physical exchanges between marked chromosomes.
Conceptual connection: scoring inherited variants supplied the genetic outcomes to compare against visible chromosome exchanges.
Conceptual connection: stable gene control extends the question of regulation to how differentiated cells maintain activity patterns through division.
Conceptual connection: methylation-based models distinguish chemical marking of DNA from alterations to its base sequence.
Studies of transferable drug resistance connected bacterial resistance patterns with the movement of genetic determinants between strains.
Conceptual connection: genetic material can cross lineage boundaries as well as pass from parent to offspring.
Darwin developed selection through mating success as part of his wider account of evolutionary change.
Conceptual connection: tracking genetic transmission allows social effects on relatives to be incorporated into evolutionary fitness accounting.
Conceptual connection: a differential equation expresses how population growth changes with population density and an imposed limiting level.
Conceptual connection: coupled rates of change model how prey availability and predator abundance modify one another’s growth.
Conceptual connection: ecological questions about interacting populations supplied a problem that coupled mathematical models could investigate.
Gause used the broader Lotka–Volterra modeling tradition to compare laboratory population interactions with mathematical predictions.
Conceptual connection: competition models extend density-dependent population growth by including the effects of another population.
Conceptual connection: immigration and extinction processes turn geographic species counts into a dynamical ecological explanation.
Conceptual connection: species’ ecological requirements constrain which arrivals can persist, although the simple island model summarizes species collectively.
Lindeman explicitly used the ecosystem as a unit for analyzing production and energy transfer.
Conceptual connection: energy accounting organizes transfer among trophic levels while distinguishing biological production from heat loss.
Conceptual connection: photosynthetic production supplies an entry point for energy into the lake food relationships Lindeman analyzed.
Hutchinson connected the niche’s multidimensional formulation with the ecological problem of competition and coexistence.
Conceptual connection: ecological study of species requirements is formalized as the combinations of conditions permitting persistence.
Conceptual connection: knowledge of organ structure makes it possible to correlate localized lesions with symptoms and clinical histories.
Conceptual connection: organ-specific lesions challenged generalized imbalance explanations without making every disease anatomically visible.
Snow’s cholera investigations challenged prevailing foul-air explanations by comparing evidence for waterborne transmission.
Conceptual connection: comparing disease frequencies in differently exposed populations supports causal investigation beyond isolated case descriptions.
Lister applied the microbial account associated with Pasteur’s research to preventing wound infection during surgery.
Conceptual connection: trials of gases and vapors tested reversible suppression of pain and awareness; no direct medieval transmission is asserted.
Conceptual connection: cultivation and observation of microorganisms made antibacterial interactions between molds and bacteria visible.
Conceptual connection: recognizing susceptible bacteria as causes of infection makes selective bacterial inhibition a therapeutic strategy.
Abraham and Chain identified an enzyme that inactivated penicillin during early investigation of the antibiotic.
Conceptual connection: inherited resistance can be favored by drug exposure; resistance mechanisms did not begin with human antibiotic use.
Conceptual connection: specific cellular targets provide a physical level at which selective drug effects can be explained.
Conceptual connection: target binding helps interpret concentration–effect relationships, although a fitted Hill curve alone does not establish a receptor mechanism.
Conceptual connection: equilibrium binding provides a mathematical route to concentration-dependent occupancy; measured responses may require additional assumptions.
Conceptual connection: circulation transports substances among tissues, motivating compartments connected by rates of transfer.
Conceptual connection: rate equations quantify distribution and elimination across connected physiological compartments.
Conceptual connection: preparing and purifying an active pancreatic substance connected metabolic experiments with hormone replacement.
Conceptual connection: connecting diabetes with pancreatic dysfunction supplied the organ-specific question addressed by pancreatic extracts.
Conceptual connection: identifying necessary dietary substances gave deficiency diseases a chemical explanation beyond calories alone.
Conceptual connection: transfusion uses the circulation, while group-specific reactions explain why exchanging blood can be incompatible.
Conceptual connection: specificity and memory are explained through selection and expansion of cells bearing suitable receptors.
Conceptual connection: selective unresponsiveness constrains theories of how antibody-producing cell populations recognize antigens.
Conceptual connection: antigen exposure can produce specific unresponsiveness under defined conditions, qualifying the expectation that exposure always promotes a response.
Conceptual connection: a selected antibody-producing cell lineage supplies the specificity retained by a hybridoma.
Conceptual connection: cultured cells can preserve and propagate a useful biological property—in this case, antibody production.
Conceptual connection: population-level transmission questions are expressed as changes among susceptible, infectious, and removed groups.
Conceptual connection: coupled rate equations connect infection and removal with depletion of susceptible individuals.
Evidence-based practice appraises clinical trials when appropriate; different clinical questions can require other study designs.
Conceptual connection: comparing populations and assessing bias underpin critical appraisal of clinical evidence.
Nowell applied heritable variation and selection to competing tumor-cell populations.
Conceptual connection: variants can exist before treatment selects among them, clarifying one route to changing tumor behavior.
The 1996 CTLA-4 experiments used antibody blockade to test whether releasing an inhibitory signal enhanced antitumor responses.
Conceptual connection: checkpoint therapies modify inhibitory regulation of adaptive immune responses to tumors.
Conceptual connection: layered rocks preserve evidence of deposition and later transformation, allowing reconstruction of crustal recycling.
Conceptual connection: repeated erosion, burial, and uplift require an Earth history extending far beyond human records.
Conceptual connection: earthquake observations and measured deformation supply the event-scale evidence that elastic rebound explains.
Conceptual connection: stored elastic strain and its release provide a mechanical account of fault displacement and seismic energy.
Holmes proposed subcrustal convection as a mechanism capable of helping explain continental movement.
Conceptual connection: radioactive heat supplied an internal-energy source relevant to Holmes’s convection argument.
Conceptual connection: motion-induced electric currents and magnetic feedback supply the physical principle of a self-sustaining fluid dynamo.
Conceptual connection: groundwater storage and movement become quantitative parts of hydrology through a flow–gradient relationship.
Conceptual connection: pressure contributes to hydraulic head, whose gradient drives flow through porous material.
Conceptual connection: rotating-frame mechanics and friction permit a mathematical balance for wind-driven ocean motion.
Conceptual connection: observed current directions become a specific explanation of wind forcing in a rotating ocean.
Conceptual connection: wind-driven rotating-ocean theory is extended from local vertical transport to circulation constrained by a basin.
Conceptual connection: spatial flow equations represent how wind, friction, and latitude-dependent rotation create an asymmetric gyre.
Conceptual connection: circulation driven by density contrasts becomes a feedback problem when transport itself changes temperature and salinity.
Conceptual connection: coupled reservoir balances allow multiple circulation equilibria to be derived under explicit idealizations.
Conceptual connection: equatorial ocean-temperature changes and currents participate in the coupled Pacific feedback described by Bjerknes.
Conceptual connection: representing interactions between climate components makes ocean–atmosphere feedback explicit; this is not a claimed transmission from one model.
Conceptual connection: changing ice coverage raises the energy-balance question of how reflected sunlight amplifies climatic shifts.
Conceptual connection: energy-balance modeling allows temperature-dependent reflectivity to be included as a climate feedback.
Conceptual connection: marine isotope records provide an independent archive for investigating repeated glacial and interglacial conditions.
Conceptual connection: sedimentary sequence places isotope measurements into an ordered record of environmental change.
Conceptual connection: hydrogen-ion concentration and acid–base equilibria explain why added carbon dioxide changes seawater pH.
Conceptual connection: uptake of anthropogenic carbon links the atmospheric carbon cycle to changes in marine carbonate chemistry.
Conceptual connection: coupled carbon-cycle calculations extend emissions scenarios into long-term projections of ocean chemistry.
Rotation supplies the sideways acceleration that balances a horizontal pressure gradient.
Spectral absorption and emission measurements constrain how gases interact with radiation at different frequencies.
Transfer equations quantify how atmospheric absorption and emission alter outgoing radiation.
Atmospheric motion is represented by fluid equations whose numerical solutions evolve in time.
Discrete time stepping approximates the evolution of a continuous atmospheric field.
Carbon exchange among rock, water, air, and organisms provides the reservoir framework.
Changes in atmospheric CO₂ connect geochemical carbon removal to radiative forcing.
Sequence analysis adds depositional boundaries and geometry to the reading of layered rocks.
Nondimensionalizing bed shear allows comparison of sediment motion across scales.
Fluid flow carries dissolved constituents through the reacting porous medium.
Rate laws describe production and consumption that cannot be treated as instantaneous equilibrium.
Tipping elements are defined as interacting subsystems within the coupled Earth system.
Positive feedback can amplify change; its existence alone does not establish a tipping threshold.
Free-energy accounting distinguishes favorable net coupling from an isolated unfavorable step.
Treating tissues as populations of individual cells makes selective cell loss a distinct process to explain.
Autophagy explains internal turnover within a living cell rather than the death of the cell as a whole.
Ordered chromosome segregation is one of the cell-cycle events that checkpoints protect.
Regulation can act on RNA processing as well as on transcription initiation.
RNA-directed silencing adds a post-transcriptional route to controlling gene output.
Locating traits on chromosomes made changes of element position experimentally interpretable.
Changing transcription-factor activity can reset regulatory networks that sustain cell identity.
A change in efficacy of transmission supplies the physical candidate for a learned connection.
Linked populations and environmental processes define the system whose persistence is assessed.
The proposal explains how innate recognition can help initiate and shape antigen-specific responses.
Antigen-specific T-cell recognition gives peptide presentation its immunological function.
Experimental study of identifiable microbes made serum-mediated killing a measurable biological question.
The intervention supplies instructions for an antigen instead of supplying a whole organism or preformed antigen.
The 2005 experiments directly examined how RNA modifications alter Toll-like receptor activation.
Inheritance of a predisposition distinguishes a germline first event from two somatic events.
Comparing viral and cellular DNA made the proposed sequence relationship experimentally testable.
Variants in handling enzymes can change drug exposure over time.
Genomic tools extend candidate-gene studies to many variants and pathways.
Water movement follows osmotic gradients created in part by solute transport.
Investigators used a viral DNA probe to detect related sequences in normal avian DNA, testing a molecular explanation for transformation.
Away from frictional layers, much large-scale horizontal flow around a gyre reflects a balance between pressure gradients and the Coriolis effect; wind stress helps drive the circulation.
Radiative–convective calculations follow absorbed and emitted energy through atmospheric layers to estimate how temperature responds to changing gas concentrations.
Weathering moves carbon between the atmosphere, oceans, and rocks. Accounting for those exchanges connects climate to solid Earth over geologic time.
ATP coupling identifies the usable chemical product; chemiosmosis explains how an ion gradient can power its synthesis across a membrane.
Correlation-based weights store patterns in a Hopfield memory. This gives a computational use for a Hebbian rule without asserting that biological synapses obey precisely that equation.
A T cell can recognize a presented peptide and still receive an inhibitory signal. Checkpoint blockade changes that brake rather than specifying which antigen the cell recognizes.
